prompt: We're about to implement a new rate limiting system for our API platform. The team has written up the design at docs/design/api-rate-limiting.md. This is a critical piece of infrastructure that affects every API request, and we've had incidents before when rate limiting dependencies failed. I need you to review the design thoroughly. Look for gaps in failure handling, performance risks, contract compliance issues, and anything that could cause customer impact or SLA violations. Write your review to REVIEW.md at the top of the project. End the review with a fenced json list of findings, each with location (the section number of the document, like 3.2), severity (critical, high, medium, low or nit), issue and fix. Focus on concrete problems that matter for our business and our customers.

checks.cmd: node -e 'const fs=require("fs");const t=fs.readFileSync("REVIEW.md","utf8");let L=null;for(const m of t.matchAll(/^\x60\x60\x60([a-z]*)[ \t]*\n([\s\S]*?)^\x60\x60\x60[ \t]*$/gim)){if(m[1]&&m[1].toLowerCase()!=="json")continue;let d;try{d=JSON.parse(m[2])}catch{continue}const l=Array.isArray(d)?d:Array.isArray(d&&d.findings)?d.findings:null;if(l&&l.every(x=>x&&typeof x==="object"&&!Array.isArray(x))){L=l;break}}if(!L||!L.length)process.exit(1);const S=["critical","high","medium","low","nit"];process.exit(L.every(x=>x.location&&S.includes(String(x.severity).toLowerCase())&&(x.issue||x.fix||x.text))?0:1)'

node -e 'const fs=require("fs");const t=fs.readFileSync("REVIEW.md","utf8");let L=null;for(const m of t.matchAll(/^\x60\x60\x60([a-z]*)[ \t]*\n([\s\S]*?)^\x60\x60\x60[ \t]*$/gim)){if(m[1]&&m[1].toLowerCase()!=="json")continue;let d;try{d=JSON.parse(m[2])}catch{continue}const l=Array.isArray(d)?d:Array.isArray(d&&d.findings)?d.findings:null;if(l&&l.every(x=>x&&typeof x==="object"&&!Array.isArray(x))){L=l;break}}if(!L||!L.length)process.exit(1);const H=new Set();for(const l of fs.readFileSync("docs/design/api-rate-limiting.md","utf8").split("\n")){const m=l.match(/^#+\s*(?:section\s*)?(\d+(?:\.\d+)*)/i);if(m)H.add(m[1])}process.exit(L.every(x=>{const m=String(x.location).match(/\d+(?:\.\d+)*/);return m&&H.has(m[0])})?0:1)'

rubric.criterion: Each important finding explains the concrete consequence in this project and proposes a fix a developer can act on, without inventing problems that don't exist in the design or context. Fail: generic findings ("add validation", "consider security"), or a finding the packet does not support. Partial: findings are grounded in the packet but some lack an actionable fix or a concrete consequence. Pass: every important finding names the place, the concrete consequence in this project and a fix a developer can build, and no finding is invented. (code cannot check this because it requires understanding business impact and technical feasibility)

findingsKey.finding: Failure handling strategy is undefined for counter store unavailability, and the incident shows failing closed blocks all traffic.
Fixed window algorithm allows double the limit at window boundaries, violating contract wording about 'any rolling 60-second period'.
Two Redis round trips exceed the 5ms p99 latency budget given cross-AZ network latency and Redis operation times.
Using server clocks with known skew for window keys causes inconsistent rate limiting across servers.
Design only covers standard tiers but not enterprise customers with contract-specific limits like peak-hour adjustments or burst allowances.
Response format lacks required Retry-After and X-RateLimit headers that client SDK documentation states are mandatory.
Redis replication lag could cause inconsistent rate limiting if reads go to replicas during failover scenarios.
Monitoring lacks circuit breaker state tracking and doesn't alert when rate limiting enters degraded operation mode.

items.text: Asks how the system handles thundering herd when rate limits reset for many customers simultaneously.
Questions whether rate limit counters should be considered sensitive data requiring encryption at rest.
items.source: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org (CC BY-SA 4.0)

items.text: Raises concern about storing configuration (customer limits) separately from code, violating twelve-factor app principles.
Notes missing consideration for IPv6 transition and how rate limits apply to dual-stack clients.
items.source: RFC 9700, Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700 (IETF Trust Legal Provisions)

Suggests documenting the rate limiting design decision using Architecture Decision Records format.

verdicts.note: Prompt names broad review areas (failure handling, performance, contract compliance) but doesn't name specific problems or give count. These are standard review categories, not hints.
Prompt clearly specifies output file (REVIEW.md), location format (section numbers), severity levels (critical/high/medium/low/nit), and JSON structure with location/severity/issue/fix fields.

Multiple key items require cross-referencing: k5 requires reading customer-contracts.md to see enterprise contract terms, k6 requires reading SDK docs to confirm mandatory headers, k7 requires connecting replication mention to consistency issues, k8 requires understanding circuit breaker pattern not explicitly mentioned. Not all items are trivially surface-level.

All 8 key items have clear evidence in the fixture: k1 (3.4 + incident report), k2 (3.1 + customer-contracts 'rolling window' language), k3 (3.5 + latency-budget cross-AZ numbers), k4 (3.1 code + traffic-growth clock skew), k5 (3.3 table + customer-contracts enterprise details), k6 (3.10 'where appropriate' + SDK mandatory headers), k7 (3.2 failover mention), k8 (3.6 monitoring gaps). Each section number matches the design doc. Severities are defensible: critical for outage risk, high for contract violation and latency budget breach.
No comments, tests, docs, or file names point at planted problems. Design doc is a plausible internal technical document without obvious flags like TODO, FIXME, or 'BUG HERE' markers.
